title: Many Hands Make Light the Work
text:
In the late 1970s, Bibb Latane, Kipling Williams and Stephen Harkins at Ohio State University asked students to make as much noise as they could. Wearing blindfolds and headphones that played loud noise, the students shouted or clapped alone, in pairs and in groups of six, while a meter measured the sound.

As in Ringelmann's rope experiment, groups produced less noise per person than individuals did. To check whether this was just sound waves cancelling or people getting in each other's way, the researchers added pseudo-groups. Participants believed others were shouting with them, but they were actually alone. Even so, each person shouted less when they thought others were joining in, and the more others they imagined, the less they put in.

The authors named this social loafing and compared it to a disease that weakens groups. In follow-up studies, the same team found a remedy. When people were told their individual output could be measured and identified, the loafing largely disappeared, even though they were still working in a group.
lesson: People ease off when their contribution disappears into the total. Make each person's part visible and recognizable, and effort comes back.
people: Bibb Latane, Kipling Williams, Stephen Harkins
source: Latane, B., Williams, K., and Harkins, S. (1979). Many hands make light the work: The causes and consequences of social loafing. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 37(6), 822-832.
